issues.legal_issue: The government is not required to constitute mining boards for every territory or class of mines before making mining regulations.
material_facts: When the regulations were framed, the Bihar Mining Board was the only validly constituted board; the boards for two other regions were not validly constituted.
The regulations were made under delegated authority, and the statutory scheme could operate without mining boards being constituted everywhere.
issues.conclusion: The provision authorizing the government to constitute mining boards is discretionary, not mandatory; the government need not constitute every board that could be relevant to proposed regulations.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 12(1) of the Mines Act, 1952, the word "may" leaves the government discretion whether to constitute a board for a territory or group or class of mines. Sections 59(3) and 59(4) require consultation with a board when one exists and is concerned or constituted for the affected territory; they do not require the government to create boards. The Court explained Banwari Lal Agarwalla v. State of Bihar, [1962] 1 S.C.R. 33, as deciding that an existing board must be consulted, not that section 12 requires boards to be constituted. The Court also relied on the functions assigned to boards under sections 14 and 81, the assumption in section 61(3) that a board might not exist, and the availability of public objections and suggestions under section 23 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.

predicates.challenge_to_validity_of_delegated_minin: A party challenged regulations made by the government under delegated authority.
predicates.board_creation_is_discretionary: The governing scheme left the government a choice whether to create a board for a territory or category of mines.
predicates.scheme_can_operate_without_boards_everyw: The mining regime could operate even if boards had not been established in every territory or for every category of mines.

issues.definition: When delegated mining regulations are challenged and the government has discretion to create boards under a scheme that can operate without boards everywhere, the government need not create every possible board.

issues.legal_issue: The consultation requirement is satisfied when an existing concerned mining board receives a reasonable opportunity to consider a draft regulation, even if its members submit individual opinions rather than a collective report.
material_facts: The government sent the draft regulations to the only validly constituted mining board through the state government.
The board's chairman circulated the draft to all board members, who communicated their opinions individually to the government.
issues.conclusion: The board was given the reasonable opportunity required by section 59(3), and individual opinions from its members did not invalidate the regulations.
issues.legal_principle: Section 59(3) of the Mines Act, 1952, required the draft to be referred to each concerned board and required that each board have a reasonable opportunity to report. It did not require the board to make a collective report, nor did it require the government to control how the board chose to respond. Banwari Lal Agarwalla v. State of Bihar, [1962] 1 S.C.R. 33, established that consultation with an existing board was mandatory; it did not prescribe the form of the board's response.

rule.if: challenge_to_mining_regulation_making and existing_concerned_board_received_draft and board_had_reasonable_opportunity and members_submitted_individual_opinions

predicates.challenge_to_mining_regulation_making: A party challenged the making of a mining regulation on the ground that the required board consultation did not occur.
predicates.existing_concerned_board_received_draft: The government sent the draft regulation to a board that existed and was concerned with its subject.
predicates.board_had_reasonable_opportunity: The board was given a reasonable opportunity to consider the draft and respond.
predicates.members_submitted_individual_opinions: The board's members communicated their views individually instead of the board submitting a collective report.

issues.definition: When an existing concerned board receives a draft and has a reasonable opportunity to respond, its members' individual opinions satisfy the consultation requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A prosecution for contravening a mining regulation cannot be quashed on the ground that the regulation was invalid where the regulation was duly framed and published after the required consultation.
material_facts: The petitioners faced a criminal prosecution for allegedly extending mine workings without the required written permission under a mining regulation.
The draft regulations had been referred to the only validly constituted concerned board, which had a reasonable opportunity to consider them, and the regulations were subsequently published.
issues.conclusion: The regulations were duly framed and published and had the effect of law; the claimed invalidity did not justify prohibiting the prosecution, and the petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 57 and 59(3) of the Mines Act, 1952, authorized regulations subject to the prescribed consultation and publication process; section 59(5) provided that published regulations had effect as if enacted in the Act. Article 20(1) did not entitle the petitioners to have the prosecution quashed on their asserted ground because the regulations were valid. The Court applied its interpretation of Banwari Lal Agarwalla v. State of Bihar, [1962] 1 S.C.R. 33, that an existing concerned board must be consulted, and held that the consultation requirement had been met.

predicates.challenge_to_criminal_prosecution_for_re: A person facing a criminal prosecution for an alleged regulatory breach sought to stop the prosecution by challenging the regulation's validity.
predicates.regulation_was_duly_published: The government completed the required process and published the regulation.
predicates.existing_concerned_board_received_reason: An existing board concerned with the regulation's subject received the draft and a reasonable opportunity to consider it.

issues.definition: When a person challenges a prosecution for a regulatory breach, a duly published regulation cannot be treated as invalid on that challenge if an existing concerned board received a reasonable opportunity to consider its draft.
